spec.title: One Mac, five controls, three verdicts
spec.intro:
You've been asked to produce an endpoint compliance-evidence packet for one Mac, built
entirely from the command line: five controls — encryption at rest, OS tamper protection,
software-execution control, central management, and an enforced screen-lock policy — each
line labeled to the control it evidences, each carrying the machine's own raw reply and a
defensible PASS / FAIL / UNKNOWN verdict. This terminal is a simulated managed Mac: the
status commands answer with the same canonical strings the lab's committed fixtures hold,
and one query path is deliberately broken so you must handle the verdict nobody likes to
write down. The discipline that carries the whole lab: a check that did not run is never
a pass — and never a clean fail.

tasks.instruction:
Get oriented (`pwd`, `ls`), then provision the lab: run `bash labs/setup.sh ./lab03`
and move into `lab03`. Look at what landed in `samples/` — committed sample replies
for every status command this lab teaches, including one deliberately empty file.
Those bytes are the lab's ground truth; CI tests against the very same files.

hints.nudge: The setup script takes a destination — §6 Setup names the exact line. `ls samples` shows what it wrote.

hints.concept: §6 Setup — the committed samples are the canonical ground truth the evaluator (and CI) test against

hints.reveal: bash labs/setup.sh ./lab03, then: cd lab03 · ls samples · cat samples/fdesetup-status.txt

tasks.explain:
Seven small files just became your reference world: known-good replies, one known-bad
reply (FileVault Off), and one empty file standing in for a query that returns nothing.
Real evaluation logic gets built against committed fixtures exactly like these — that's
how the module's own CI proves the lab works with no Mac attached.

tasks.instruction:
Ask the two foundational subsystems directly. Run `fdesetup status`, then
`csrutil status`. Before each: name the control whose truth you're asking for and the
subsystem that owns it (§3 map). After each: read the reply against the §4 known-good
string and state your verdict.

hints.nudge: Encryption-at-rest truth lives in FileVault (§4.1); OS-tamper-protection truth lives in SIP (§4.2). One canonical status command each.

hints.concept: §3 — name the subsystem that owns the claim first; only then reach for the command that reads it

tasks.explain:
`FileVault is On.` is the same laptop-encryption claim you counted across a fleet in
module 01 — here you're standing on the endpoint where that truth physically lives,
asking the owning subsystem directly. And SIP's `enabled` is the control beneath the
controls: it's why the machine's other answers about itself can be trusted at all.

tasks.instruction:
Replies you only looked at are not evidence. Create `evidence/`, then capture four raw
replies as kept artifacts using `tee`: FileVault → `evidence/filevault.txt`, Gatekeeper
(`spctl --status`) → `evidence/gatekeeper.txt`, MDM enrollment
(`profiles status -type enrollment`) → `evidence/mdm.txt`, and installed profiles
(`system_profiler SPConfigurationProfileDataType`) → `evidence/profiles.txt`.

hints.nudge: `tee` is the §5.1 move — the reply still prints to your screen AND lands in the file. The directory has to exist first.

hints.concept: §5.1 — keep the machine's own reply as the artifact, not a screenshot of it

hints.reveal: mkdir evidence, then: fdesetup status | tee evidence/filevault.txt · spctl --status | tee evidence/gatekeeper.txt · profiles status -type enrollment | tee evidence/mdm.txt · system_profiler SPConfigurationProfileDataType | tee evidence/profiles.txt

tasks.explain:
Four files now hold raw machine replies, each produced by the subsystem that owns the
claim — and the checker verified not just the bytes but the provenance: each artifact
had to come from its real query piped through `tee`, not from an editor. Re-run any of
those lines next quarter and compare byte-for-byte: that's evidence, not a screenshot.

tasks.instruction:
Write the evaluator, `evaluate.sh`. It takes three arguments — a raw reply, a
known-good pattern, a known-bad pattern — and prints exactly one word. The §4.8 shape,
in order: empty (or whitespace-only) reply means the check could not run → `UNKNOWN`,
asked FIRST; else a known-good match → `PASS`; else a known-bad match → `FAIL`; else
→ `UNKNOWN`. Spell the conditions with `test` (the spelled-out form of `[` — this lab
box's zsh layer chokes on the bare bracket). Make it executable, then prove it on
three samples: FileVault On (`PASS`), FileVault Off (`FAIL`), and
`samples/profiles-status-unknown.txt` — the empty one, which must print `UNKNOWN`,
not `FAIL`. The checker also re-runs your script in a clean room against hidden
vectors, including a garbage reply that matches neither pattern.

hints.nudge: Two questions in order, then a default: known-good → PASS, else known-bad → FAIL, else UNKNOWN. And ask "is it empty?" before either — strip whitespace with `tr -d`, test the remainder with `test -z`.

hints.concept: §4.8 / §5.2 — a check that did not run is never a pass and never a clean fail

hints.reveal: nano evaluate.sh — take the raw reply, good and bad patterns as "$1" "$2" "$3". First condition: test -z on "$(printf '%s' "$raw" | tr -d '[:space:]')" prints UNKNOWN (the could-not-run gate). Next: printf '%s' "$raw" | grep -Eqi -- "$good" prints PASS. Next: the same grep against "$bad" prints FAIL. The final else prints UNKNOWN. Save, chmod +x evaluate.sh, then run ./evaluate.sh "$(cat samples/profiles-status-unknown.txt)" 'MDM enrollment: Yes' 'MDM enrollment: No' — it must say UNKNOWN

tasks.explain:
The order of those questions is the whole §4.8 lesson. An evaluator that asks
"known-good, else FAIL" silently converts a permission error or an unmanaged device
into a clean finding — or worse, a clean pass. Yours asked "did the check even run?"
first, so the empty reply surfaced as UNKNOWN: a gap a human must investigate, not a
verdict a machine invented. The clean-room re-run also proved it's deterministic.

tasks.instruction:
Compose the packet. Write `collect-endpoint-evidence.sh`: capture each subsystem's
reply with command substitution, pass each through `$HOME/lab03/evaluate.sh` with that
control's known-good/known-bad strings, and echo one labeled line per control in the
§5.4 shape `CONTROL: … | SUBSYSTEM: … | VERDICT: … | RAW: …`. Include the sixth,
deliberately broken query — read `samples/profiles-status-unknown.txt`; when it's
empty, send a `WARN:` line ending "returned nothing" to stderr and let the verdict
fall out as UNKNOWN. The screen-lock control passes only when BOTH the MDM verdict and
the profile-payload verdict pass (§5.3). Two craft rules: multi-line replies get
reduced to their verdict-bearing line (pipe through `grep`) so every packet line stays
one line; use absolute paths (`$HOME/lab03/…`) — the script can't assume where its
runner stands. Make it executable and run it with stdout to `evidence/packet.txt` and
stderr to `collection-errors.log`.

hints.nudge: One $( ) per subsystem query, one echo per control — and each line's verdict is itself a $( ) call into your evaluator. stderr is a separate channel: `2>` carries only the complaints.

hints.concept: §5.4 — every packet line names the control, the subsystem that owns its truth, the three-valued verdict, and the raw reply that justifies it

hints.reveal: nano collect-endpoint-evidence.sh — capture FV="$(fdesetup status)", SIP="$(csrutil status)", GK="$(spctl --status)", MDM="$(profiles status -type enrollment | grep 'MDM enrollment')", PROF="$(system_profiler SPConfigurationProfileDataType | grep 'askForPassword')", GAP="$(cat "$HOME/lab03/samples/profiles-status-unknown.txt")". When test -z finds "$GAP" empty, echo "WARN: profile sample query returned nothing" >&2. Each packet line follows echo "CONTROL: Encryption at rest (CC6.1) | SUBSYSTEM: FileVault | VERDICT: $("$HOME/lab03/evaluate.sh" "$FV" 'FileVault is On' 'FileVault is Off') | RAW: $FV" — six lines: FileVault, SIP, Gatekeeper, MDM, screen-lock (PASS only when the MDM verdict and the payload verdict are both PASS), and the sample-gap line evaluated from "$GAP". Then chmod +x collect-endpoint-evidence.sh and ./collect-endpoint-evidence.sh > evidence/packet.txt 2> collection-errors.log

tasks.explain:
Six labeled lines, five PASS, one UNKNOWN — and the operational complaint went to its
own log, so the packet stayed clean machine-readable data. The checker verified the
verdicts against the seeded device state, the stream separation, and the provenance:
the packet had to be produced by your collector, not assembled by hand. This artifact
IS the module: LOCATE the subsystem, QUERY it, evaluate honestly, keep the raw reply.

tasks.instruction:
Prove the packet is deterministic. Run the collector again into
`evidence/packet2.txt` (append stderr with `2>>`), then `diff` the two packets and
inspect `$?` — silence and a zero are your proof. The checker goes further: it
re-runs your script twice in a clean room with the clock deliberately skewed between
runs, so determinism has to be a property of YOUR script, not of running it twice
quickly.

hints.nudge: `diff a b` says nothing when the files agree — its verdict lives in `$?`.

hints.concept: §4.8 / §5.4 — identical bytes on re-run is what turns a report into a monitorable control

hints.reveal: ./collect-endpoint-evidence.sh > evidence/packet2.txt 2>> collection-errors.log, then: diff evidence/packet.txt evidence/packet2.txt · echo $?

tasks.explain:
Identical evidence, twice — and the clean-room re-run proved it wasn't luck. A packet
that re-runs identically can be scheduled, compared, and alerted on; one with a
timestamp or a random ordering inside can't. Module 13 will put exactly this property
on a schedule and catch drift with it.

tasks.instruction:
Surface the gap. Pull the UNKNOWN line out of the packet with `grep`. That line is
not a flaw in the packet — it's the packet doing its job: telling you exactly which
control's truth could not be established so a human follows up.

hints.nudge: The packet is grep-able by design — that's why the labels are machine-shaped.

tasks.explain:
One control's truth could not be established, and your packet says so out loud. Had
the evaluator scored it PASS, a real gap would be hidden; had it scored it FAIL, a
human would chase a false finding. UNKNOWN routes the right person to the right
question — that's the difference between an analyst and an auditor.

tasks.instruction:
The map, from memory (§6 task 1): for each of the five controls — encryption at rest,
OS tamper protection, software-execution control, central management, enforced
screen lock — name the subsystem that owns its truth and the command that reads it.
Then explain, in 2–3 sentences for an auditor with no Mac background, WHERE the claim
"this laptop's disk is encrypted" physically lives and why the screen-lock control
needs two subsystems to answer (§5.3).

hints.nudge: §3's stack of trust, bottom-up: SIP → FileVault → Gatekeeper → (TCC/Keychain/launchd) → MDM. The screen-lock answer needs enrollment AND the installed payload.

hints.concept: §3 — seven subsystems, seven slices of control-truth; MDM is the claim that the other claims are governed

tasks.instruction:
Two sentences on the UNKNOWN line (§6 task 7): which control's truth couldn't be
established, and why scoring it as PASS or as a clean FAIL would each have been a
defect. Then one sentence connecting "the packet came out byte-identical twice" to
continuous monitoring (§6 task 6).

hints.nudge: PASS hides a real gap; FAIL invents a finding. And evidence you can re-run identically is evidence you can schedule.

hints.concept: §4.8 — UNKNOWN is a result you surface, not swallow; §5.4 — re-runnable packets are what continuous assurance is made of

files.content:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Module 03 lab fixture generator (original lab asset).
# Usage: setup.sh [DEST_DIR]   (default ./lab03)
# Produces a samples/ directory of representative *sample outputs* of the macOS status
# commands taught in this module. These let a learner (or CI on Linux) build and test the
# control-EVALUATION logic with NO macOS machine and NO macOS-only binaries. Each file is
# what the corresponding command prints; one file is deliberately empty to exercise UNKNOWN.
set -euo pipefail
DEST="${1:-./lab03}"
S="$DEST/samples"
mkdir -p "$S"

# FileVault ON  -> encryption-at-rest PASS
printf '%s\n' 'FileVault is On.' > "$S/fdesetup-status.txt"

# FileVault OFF -> encryption-at-rest FAIL (the explicit negative fixture)
printf '%s\n' 'FileVault is Off.' > "$S/fdesetup-status-off.txt"

# SIP enabled -> OS-tamper-protection PASS
printf '%s\n' 'System Integrity Protection status: enabled.' > "$S/csrutil-status.txt"

# Gatekeeper assessments enabled -> software-execution-control PASS
printf '%s\n' 'assessments enabled' > "$S/spctl-status.txt"

# MDM enrolled -> centrally-managed PASS
{
  printf '%s\n' 'Enrolled via DEP: Yes'
  printf '%s\n' 'MDM enrollment: Yes (User Approved)'
} > "$S/profiles-status.txt"

# Installed configuration profiles incl. a screen-lock policy payload -> policy-present
{
  printf '%s\n' 'Configuration Profiles:'
  printf '%s\n' '    ScreenLock Policy:'
  printf '%s\n' '        Payloads: com.apple.screensaver (askForPassword=1, idleTime=600)'
} > "$S/system_profiler-profiles.txt"

# A check that COULD NOT RUN: empty output. Must evaluate to UNKNOWN, never PASS/FAIL.
: > "$S/profiles-status-unknown.txt"

echo "lab03 fixtures written to $S/"

tools.profiles:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Simulated MDM-enrollment query for the module 03 lab box (§4.7).
# Output is canon-locked to modules/03-macos-fundamentals/labs/setup.sh
# (samples/profiles-status.txt) — the module's committed ground truth for the
# enrolled, User-Approved-MDM scenario Mac. The module's own prose marks real
# `profiles` output "representative"; the committed fixture strings are what the
# lab's evaluator and CI (labs/happy-path.sh) test against, so the simulator
# reproduces the FIXTURES byte-exactly (manifest entry m03-profiles-status).
# NOTE: written with `case`/`test` (no bare `[`) — the lab box is the zsh variant.
case "${1:-} ${2:-} ${3:-}" in
  "status -type enrollment")
    printf '%s\n' 'Enrolled via DEP: Yes'
    printf '%s\n' 'MDM enrollment: Yes (User Approved)'
    ;;
  *)
    echo "profiles: only 'profiles status -type enrollment' is on this lab's simulated surface — run it on a real Mac to explore" >&2
    exit 64
    ;;
esac
tools.system_profiler:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Simulated configuration-profile enumeration for the module 03 lab box (§4.7).
# Output is canon-locked to modules/03-macos-fundamentals/labs/setup.sh
# (samples/system_profiler-profiles.txt) — the module's committed ground truth for
# the scenario Mac with the ScreenLock Policy payload installed. Real
# `system_profiler SPConfigurationProfileDataType` output is richer and
# host-specific (the module prose says "representative and abbreviated"); the
# committed fixture is the canon the evaluator and CI test against, so the
# simulator reproduces it byte-exactly (manifest entry m03-system-profiler-profiles).
# NOTE: written with `case`/`test` (no bare `[`) — the lab box is the zsh variant.
case "${1:-}" in
  SPConfigurationProfileDataType)
    printf '%s\n' 'Configuration Profiles:'
    printf '%s\n' '    ScreenLock Policy:'
    printf '%s\n' '        Payloads: com.apple.screensaver (askForPassword=1, idleTime=600)'
    ;;
  *)
    echo "system_profiler: only the SPConfigurationProfileDataType data type is on this lab's simulated surface — run it on a real Mac to explore" >&2
    exit 64
    ;;
esac
tools.launchctl:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Honest sim boundary (web ISA ISC-120). Module 03 §4.6 teaches `launchctl list`,
# so the binary must EXIST on the simulated Mac (a real Mac always has it) — but its
# output is host-specific and the module's committed fixture canon doesn't pin it,
# so simulating a reply would be invention. The stub answers with the lab's standard
# boundary message instead of a false `command not found`.
# NOTE: written with `case`/`test` (no bare `[`) — the lab box is the zsh variant.
echo "launchctl: not on this lab's simulated surface (§4.6 teaches the concept) — run it on a real Mac to explore" >&2
exit 64
tools.security:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Honest sim boundary (web ISA ISC-120). Module 03 §4.5 teaches `security list-keychains`,
# so the binary must EXIST on the simulated Mac (a real Mac always has it) — but keychain
# listings are host-specific and the module's committed fixture canon doesn't pin them,
# so simulating a reply would be invention. The stub answers with the lab's standard
# boundary message instead of a false `command not found`.
# NOTE: written with `case`/`test` (no bare `[`) — the lab box is the zsh variant.
echo "security: not on this lab's simulated surface (§4.5 teaches the concept) — run it on a real Mac to explore" >&2
exit 64
